To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the covalently bound UV filter molecules that accumulate in the aging lens are primarily derived from kynurenine UV filters, and that these are bound to lens proteins via Michael addition of the reactive alpha,beta-unsaturated keto group of the filter molecule to nucleophilic sites on the protein.
glutathione and NADAH, but not vitamin C, are effective at inhibiting the covalent modification of lens crystallins by UV filters.

glutathione, but not aspartate, protects lens crystallins against covalent modification by UV filters, and that this is due to the ability of glutathione to intercept the reactive alpha,beta-unsaturated ketone intermediate formed during the deamination of kynurenine.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the chemical mechanisms underlying age-dependent lens colouration.
understanding the chemical basis of the age-related yellowing and fluorescence of the lens.
the covalent modification of lens proteins by UV filters, and the role of small molecular weight lens antioxidants in this process.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the antioxidant properties of GSH and NADH are responsible for protecting the human lens proteins from modification, whereas the antioxidant ascorbate has no effect.
the lens is well equipped to protect its crystallins from the deleterious effects of UV filters.
GSH, but not as ascorbate, is the major small-molecular-weight antioxidant in the lens that is capable of inhibiting Kyn binding to crystallins.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the covalently-bound Kyn molecules are likely to have originated from UV filters, and are not likely to be a result of endogenous metabolism.
the age-related yellowing and fluorescence of the lens are primarily caused by the covalent modification of lens proteins by UV filters.
the covalently attached Kyn in primate lenses is a consequence of the low levels of GSH in the older human lens, which are insufficient to prevent the deamination of Kyn.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the age-dependent accumulation of Kyn in human lenses may be the result of a combination of the inability of the lens to remove Kyn, and the failure of GSH and NADH to prevent Kyn binding to crystallins.
GSH is the primary agent responsible for protecting crystallins from co-valent modification by Kyn and other UV filters.
GSH, but not NADH or ascorbate, is a major protective agent against the covalent modification of crystallins by the UV filter Kyn.
